## Catholic
Peter himself is the rock. Jesus gives Simon a new name and then builds on him, so the Church rests on Peter's person and office, which passes to the bishops of Rome who succeed him. The weight falls on the wordplay between Peter and rock, read as one and the same, and on the promise that Hades will not prevail. It takes the words as Jesus' own words, spoken as the Gospel reports them, and the promise as a real act of Christ; it holds the Bible fully true and reads it with the Church's tradition. Held by the Catholic Church.

The reading also hears the keys and the binding and loosing of the verses that follow as given to the same man, so that the one office founded here is the one exercised in them, and it takes the Church's long practice of reading the three gifts together as a guide to what the words were meant to found. On this reading the passage is the charter of a visible, ordered Church, and Rome's claim stands or falls with it.

## Eastern Orthodox
The rock is Peter's confession in the verse before, and Peter as the one who confesses it. Many of the Fathers read it so, and Orthodox teaching holds that every bishop who keeps that confession sits in Peter's seat, so the verse founds the Church on right faith and on the whole episcopate. The weight falls on the confession and on the shift from Petros to petra. It takes the saying as Jesus' own words and the promise as real, holds the Bible fully true, and reads it with the Fathers. Held by the Orthodox Church.

The reading points to the whole scene: the question put to the Twelve, the answer given by one of them, and the blessing that names Simon as the one to whom the Father has shown it, so that the rock is the faith confessed and the man confessing it, together and never apart. It takes the promise to the assembly as a promise to every local church that keeps that faith, and reads the keys as given to the apostles as a body.

## Reformed
The rock is Christ, confessed by Peter, who speaks for all the apostles; the Church is built on that confession, so no single office is founded here. The weight falls on the change of word from Petros to petra and on Scripture read with Scripture, where Christ is the one foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11) and the living stone (1 Peter 2:4–8). It takes the words as Jesus' own words and the promise as a real act of Christ; it holds the Bible fully true and the text alone as its authority. Held by Reformed and Presbyterian churches, and by most evangelical churches.

The reading sets the verse beside the letters, where the apostles and prophets are the foundation and Christ himself the chief cornerstone, and beside the saying that whoever hears these words and does them builds on the rock; it takes the figure of building on rock as a figure for faith in Christ, used across the Gospel, and so hears the assembly founded on the confession rather than on the confessor.

## Historical-critical
The saying is read as a later composition: Matthew's community reflecting on Peter's standing after his death, since Matthew alone uses the word assembly and alone records this promise. Some scholars defend it as an original saying, perhaps in Aramaic, where one word, Kepha, would stand for both name and rock. It treats the Gospel as a human record shaped by the community that kept it, and scholarly reconstruction as its authority. Held by critical scholars of several churches and of none, who are divided among themselves.

The reading weighs the silence of the other Gospels, where the confession is given without the promise, and the word assembly, which this Gospel uses twice and the others never, as signs of the evangelist's own shaping of the scene for a community that by then had the makings of an ordered life. It reads the promise that Hades will not prevail as that community's confidence in its own survival, set in the mouth of Jesus by the one who wrote the Gospel.

## Where they agree
All four read Peter as spokesman for the apostles' confession, the assembly as the one people Jesus gathers, and the gates of Hades as the power of death, which cannot destroy it.

## Where they part, and why
- Whether Petros and petra name the same thing: one rock for the Catholic reading, a shift that matters for the others, and for the historical-critical reading a shift the Greek made when it rendered one Aramaic word twice.
- Whether what is founded is an office that passes on, a confession kept by all bishops, or the confession as such; the first two read the verse with what the Church later did, the third reads it with the rest of the New Testament.
- Whether the words are Jesus' own or the community's: a question about the Gospel itself, and the one difference that no reading of the Greek can close.
- What settles it: tradition, the Fathers, Scripture read with Scripture, or reconstruction; each reading names its authority, and the authorities do not overlap.

## What the text settles
The wordplay is in the text, and the confession stands in the verse before it, so a reading that separates the rock from the confession rests on little here. The Greek has two forms, Petros and petra, and the passage does not say whether the change is meant; a reader who knows no Greek still sees that the name and the rock are set side by side on purpose. Nothing in the verse speaks of succession, for or against, and nothing in it names Rome, a see or an office that outlives the man addressed. The gates of Hades are the power of death, so the promise is that the assembly survives, not that it never errs.

## Questions to take back to the text
1. Read verses 13 to 20 together: does the promise answer the man or the confession?
2. In your translation, is rock the same word as Peter, and what changes if it is?
3. What does Jesus build, an assembly, and who belongs to it elsewhere in this Gospel?
4. What did you bring to this verse: which reading did you expect, and where did it come from?
